title: Japanese M 3+ earthquakes had fewer earlier M 2 events nearby per magnitude unit (JMA 2000-2024), half the global ComCat deficit; it is in same-day bursts, not mixed magnitude types
abstract: We tested the campaign result that larger shallow earthquakes have fewer small earlier events nearby (global ComCat, beta -0.175 per magnitude unit) with an independent catalog: the JMA unified hypocenter catalog of Japan, 1998-2024. We wrote the plan before we computed outcomes. Targets were 41,564 M 3.0+ events (depth 70 km or less, 2000-2024) with no earlier M 3+ event within 20 km and 30 days. We counted M 2.0-2.9 events within 10 km in the 30 days before each target and fitted a conditional Poisson model with 0.5 degree cell x era strata and a background term. Result: beta = -0.090 (stratum bootstrap 95% interval -0.145 to -0.034; permutation p = 0.004). The sign agrees with the global result, but the interval excludes -0.175. Forty magnitude-shuffle catalogs, which keep the real space-time pattern, gave mean beta near 0 (SD 0.016-0.021). The deficit was largest within 3-5 km (-0.21, -0.17) and 1 h to 1 day before the target (-0.33, SE 0.10), and it was in M 3.0-3.9 targets (-0.14, SE 0.05), not clearly in M 4+ targets (-0.03, SE 0.06). Mixed magnitude types do not explain it: with velocity magnitudes for all targets, beta = -0.10, and the displacement-minus-velocity magnitude offset did not change with earlier activity. Strata of 0.1 degree, history covariates, an incompleteness guard, a lower band and both periods gave the same sign. The global setup inside Japan (M 5+ targets, band M 4.5-4.9) gave -0.15 (SE 0.14), so Japan cannot confirm or reject the global value at large magnitudes. Post hoc, targets after a same-day burst were more often followed by a larger event within 10 km and 7 days (15.3% against 3.9%), but magnitude-shuffle catalogs gave a larger ratio (log rate ratio 1.68 against 1.78-2.49), so bursts were not better precursors than clustering predicts. We interpret the result as slightly smaller events in short local bursts (a transient higher b-value), not a preparation process. Limitations: two Mj types, offshore incompleteness, a shuffle null in place of a fitted ETAS model, few large targets, and uncorrected post-hoc tests. Raw JMA records stay external; code, aggregate results and figures are included.

citations.reason: Independent regional test of its global result: the sign replicates in JMA, the size is about half, and the magnitude-type explanation is excluded for Japan. We reuse its cpois.py and five published class ratios.
Felzer et al. 2004: no magnitude dependence of foreshock numbers; our M 4+ results agree.
Lippiello et al. 2012: magnitude-dependent foreshock activity; we find the opposite sign for M 3-4 targets.
